details:
**Rhea's stone**
Cronus swallowed each of his children at birth to prevent a prophecy that one would overthrow him. When Zeus was born, his mother Rhea hid him and gave Cronus a stone wrapped in swaddling clothes to swallow instead; Zeus later forced Cronus to vomit up his siblings Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades, and Poseidon.

**Amalthea and the Kouretes on Mount Ida**
The infant Zeus was hidden in a cave on Mount Ida in Crete, where he was nursed by the goat (or nymph) Amalthea and fed honey by nymphs such as the daughters of Melisseus. The Kouretes (Curetes) clashed their shields and spears to drown out his crying, and the Dactyls, born when Rhea pressed her fingers into the earth, also watched over him. In one version he was hung from a tree so that Cronus, who ruled sky, earth, and sea, could not find him.

**Europa and the white bull**
Zeus transformed into a beautiful white bull to abduct the Phoenician princess Europa, carrying her on his back across the sea to Crete. There she bore him Minos, Rhadamanthus, and Sarpedon, and Zeus gave her gifts including the bronze giant Talos, the hound Laelaps, and a javelin that never missed.

**Ganymede and the eagle**
Zeus took the form of an eagle (or sent his eagle) to carry off the beautiful Trojan shepherd boy Ganymede, who became cupbearer of the gods on Olympus. Zeus compensated Ganymede's father Tros with divine horses and later placed Ganymede in the stars as Aquarius. He also abducted the nymph Aegina as an eagle.

**Leda and the swan**
Zeus seduced the Spartan queen Leda in the form of a swan. She bore eggs from which came Helen and Polydeuces (Pollux), and in many versions Castor and Clytemnestra.

**Danae and the golden shower**
King Acrisius of Argos locked his daughter Danae in an underground bronze chamber after an oracle said her son would kill him. Zeus came to her as a shower of gold, and she gave birth to the hero Perseus.

**Metis and the birth of Athena**
Zeus's first wife Metis was prophesied to bear a son who would overthrow him, so Zeus tricked her into turning into a fly and swallowed her. He later suffered a terrible headache, and when Hephaestus (or Prometheus) split his head open with an axe, Athena sprang out fully armed.

**Semele and Dionysus**
Hera tricked the Theban princess Semele into asking Zeus to reveal his true divine form, and she was incinerated by his radiance. Zeus rescued the unborn Dionysus and sewed him into his thigh until he was ready to be born.

**Titanomachy, Kampe, and the Hundred-Handers**
To win the ten-year war against Cronus and the Titans, Zeus killed the dragon-woman Kampe, the jailer of Tartarus, and freed the Cyclopes and the Hecatoncheires (Briareos, Cottus, and Gyges). After victory, he and his brothers divided the cosmos, with Zeus taking the sky.

**Thunderbolt**
Zeus's signature weapon, forged for him by the Cyclopes, who also made Poseidon's trident and Hades's helm of invisibility. He used it to strike down figures such as Phaethon (who lost control of Helios's chariot), the healer Asclepius, and Salmoneus, a king who impersonated Zeus by driving his chariot over a bronze bridge to mimic thunder.

**Typhon**
A monstrous serpentine giant who challenged Zeus and, in one version, cut out Zeus's sinews and hid them in a cave. Hermes and Aegipan recovered the sinews, and Zeus defeated Typhon with thunderbolts and buried him beneath Mount Etna.

**Lycaon**
An Arcadian king who tested Zeus's divinity by serving him human flesh. Zeus turned him into a wolf, and the cult of Zeus Lykaios on Mount Lykaion was associated with human sacrifice and werewolf legends; Zeus's anger at mankind's wickedness also led to the great flood that only Deucalion and Pyrrha survived.

**Statue of Zeus at Olympia**
A colossal gold-and-ivory (chryselephantine) statue of the seated Zeus made by Phidias for the temple at Olympia, holding a figure of Nike in his right hand. It was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World; the Zanes were bronze statues of Zeus near the Olympic stadium paid for by fines on cheating athletes.

**Baucis and Philemon**
An elderly Phrygian couple who hospitably fed Zeus and Hermes when they visited in disguise, after everyone else had turned them away. As Zeus Xenios, god of xenia (hospitality to guests), he spared them from a flood and turned them into an intertwined oak and linden tree at their deaths.

**Callisto and other disguises**
Zeus disguised himself as Artemis to seduce her follower Callisto, mother of Arcas. He also became a dove to seduce Phthia and turned Eurymedousa into an ant, and he punished the nymph Chelone, who refused to attend his wedding to Hera, by turning her into a tortoise.
